title: Letter 10 — On the Love of Money, the Root of All Evils
attribution_note: Letter 10 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: I wrote to you before of certain things; now I write of what the apostle calls “the root of all evils,” and of who may truly be called rich. And at the outset I set down the apostle's word concerning “those who will be rich,” of whom the apostle speaks thus: *“They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition: for the love of money is the root of all evil”* [1 Timothy 6:9–10]. Attend, then, to the following points, and you will see it for yourself.
1) The lust of riches is not only in itself evil and harmful, but is the cause of every evil. It arms a man against all the commandments of God, and teaches him to break every one of them.

Against the first commandment: *“I am the Lord thy God.”* It turns a man away from obedience, from hope in God, and brings him into fearlessness. Many gather riches for this very purpose, that by their help they may escape the misfortunes that come upon them, and in the calamity that befalls them they say to their treasure: thou art my hope — which happens above all in these present times, when gold and silver lift up their voice in court, while the truth is silent. And so the apostle exhorts: *“Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God”* [1 Timothy 6:17].

Against the second: *“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image.”* *“Covetousness is idolatry”* [Colossians 3:5], and *“the covetous man is an idolater”* [Ephesians 5:5]. Covetousness is the lust and the love of riches. How many betray and enrol themselves as the devil's own, and worship him as slaves, for the sake of riches!

Against the third: *“Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain.”* How many, coming into power and becoming judges, swear falsely, and having sworn, break their oath, and so *“take”* the great and dread *“name of God in vain,”* for the sake of riches — many thousands bear witness to this. How many merchants swear fearlessly and lawlessly by the name of God that their wares are worth so much and so much, when in truth it is otherwise, and so lie, and dishonour the holy name of God for the sake of gain! O evil lust! To what does it bring the poor man! It teaches him to call upon the great and dread name of God falsely, in vain, and for the sake of some vile profit!

Against the fourth: *“Remember the sabbath day,”* and the rest. How many, on the feast days set apart for divine worship, leave the church and the service for the sake of gain, and do whatever their lust desires!

Against the fifth: *“Honour thy father,”* and the rest. How many children abandon their parents, and do not help them in their need and their old age, lest their own estate suffer loss, and become *“worse than infidels”* [1 Timothy 5:8]! How many there are who, for the sake of silver and gold, betray and sell their fatherland, and in it their own houses, and their own parents, wives and children! Read the histories, and you will see it. And would that this were not so today!

Against the sixth: *“Thou shalt not kill.”* How many kill for the sake of silver and gold, and do not spare men like themselves, made in the image of God, and shed innocent blood! How many turn to robbery!
Against the seventh: *“Thou shalt not commit adultery.”* How many wives and maidens have become, and become, open harlots for the gathering of riches — the histories bear witness to this.

Against the eighth: *“Thou shalt not steal.”* It is impossible to number how many deceits, open and secret plunderings, this lust devises, so that scarcely anyone is free of them — merchants, powerful men, the rich, those clothed with authority and those who serve them, those who sit in the courts, and the clerks of the chanceries, above all others. Truly someone once wrote: “The world is filled with thieves.”

Against the ninth: *“Thou shalt not bear false witness.”* How many are bribed with silver and gold, and speak falsehood in the courts, and so sell truth and justice for gain, and justify the guilty, and condemn the innocent and the just! So the guards at the Lord's tomb, bribed by the chief priests, spoke falsely and against their own conscience, that His disciples had stolen Him by night while they slept, and concealed the truth of His Resurrection [Matthew 28:15].

Against the tenth: *“Thou shalt not covet.”* What that belongs to another does this lust not covet? It wants everything for itself, to have in its own house. It casts its eyes on everything that belongs to another. See, then, the root of all evil! Cut off the root, then, and its evil branches will wither. Renounce the lust, and you will not fall into evil. “Thou shalt not covet” — be content with what you have, and you will be free of evils.

2) Guard yourself against this plague, which puts both soul and body to death forever [1 Corinthians 6:10; Ephesians 5:5], and look about you carefully, to see whether it is not in you, since it is a hidden thing. The lust of fornication and the passion for drunkenness are plain to see, but no man has ever yet called himself a lover of money. Yet, as you have seen, there are few in whom this passion is not found. Examine yourself carefully, then, to see whether it is not nesting in your heart. And here is the remedy for escaping it: think, and remember, that you will leave in the world everything that is gathered here, and that piety alone will go with you when you depart from the world, of which more below.

3) As all men enter the world equally — that is, naked and needy — so all go out of the world equally, save only that one departs a sinner, and another righteous. *“For we brought nothing into this world; and it is certain we can carry nothing out”* — so says the apostle [1 Timothy 6:7]. And Job said: *“Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return”* [Job 1:21]. And life itself shows this. Where the rich man lies in the earth after death, and where the poor man, where the master and where the servant, it is impossible to tell. Here, then, is a remedy against the lust of the love of money: you will go out from the world with nothing, and appear before the Lord — only take care that you do not appear before Him with that lust. It will itself accuse you and condemn you before Him, and will show what your heart was occupied with in the world, what you loved and what you sought — God, or silver. Remember this, and that lust will depart from you. Blessed and wise is he who says with Job: “Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return” there, whither all who live upon the earth are going!

sections.heading: Who is rich, and who is poor

pairs.en: 4) Who is rich, and who is poor? He is rich who desires no more, but is content with what he has; and he who desires more and more is poor. We call a man full who does not wish to eat, and hungry the one who does. So he ought to be called rich who desires nothing further, and poor who desires more riches. It is not the storehouse, nor the coffers, nor the purse that is called rich, but the man. Therefore whoever has even empty coffers and an empty storehouse, but is content with what he has, is rich; and whoever has coffers full, but desires more, is poor and needy, for he has nothing in his heart — and he has nothing, because he desires. Much is lacking to him who desires much; little is lacking to him who desires little; nothing is needful to him who desires nothing. If he has something, it is well; if he has nothing, that too is well: he is content whether he has or has not, whether he is rich or poor. Food and clothing are his sufficiency. Blessed is such a heart! This man is a wayfarer and a stranger in this world.

5) Only the godly are rich, as the apostle Paul bears witness: *“Godliness with contentment is great gain”* [1 Timothy 6:6]. What does “gain” mean? The same as riches, treasure. What does it mean, “to be content”? To be content with what you have, whether little or great, whether much or little (of this it was said above, in the fourth point). He has a great treasure who has godliness. Why? Because he has a treasure incomparably better than the treasure of this world; and he has it within himself, not outside himself; and he has it inalienably, and it is with him now, and with him in death, and with him after death. And what treasure is this? A living faith, the knowledge and reverence of God, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and the hope of the eternal inheritance in the heavens — all that is contained in godliness. This, then, is the treasure and the riches of the godly! Having set their hope on God, they are content with God, as the highest good, than whom there is no greater good, and from whom every good proceeds. God is to them *“a great reward,”* riches, treasure and glory, and in the life of blessedness *“He shall be all in all”* [1 Corinthians 15:28].

The ungodly have riches — that is, corruptible and fleeting riches — as it were in a dream, and are therefore poor and needy; and having left behind all that with which they were content, as though in a dream, they will come to such poverty that they will desire a single drop of water for all eternity, and no one will give it them, as we see in the example of the rich man in the Gospel [Luke 16:24]. And the Lord confirms this, saying: *“What is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away”* [Matthew 16:26]? Though the ungodly are rich, they are rich in their storehouses and their coffers, and not in themselves, and that only as in a dream. Yesterday, and all time past, is to us as a dream, and so the riches of this world will be as a dream after death. Whoever sees something in a dream, sees it only while he sleeps, but on waking sees nothing, and remembers only the dream. So it is with the rich man: while he lives, he sees his riches; but when he dies, it all departs from him like a dream, and he has nothing left to himself but memory and an evil conscience, for he *“laid up treasure for himself, and was not rich toward God”* [Luke 12:21].

sections.heading: Treasure that does not vanish like a dream

pairs.en: Not so the godly, not so! They are rich here, and there they will be richest of all. Here too they *“have”* and carry their *“treasure”* *“in earthen vessels”* [2 Corinthians 4:7], and there they will inherit those good things which *“eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man”* [1 Corinthians 2:9]. That riches, then, is the true riches, which is within a man, and does not depart from him, and goes with him from here into that age — and this riches is godliness. And only he is rich who has within himself the treasure of godliness.

6) Let us strive, brethren, to have this treasure, and not that which departs from us, and so often hinders us from seeking the true treasure of which the Lord speaks: *“Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal”* [Matthew 6:20]. Let us not look, then, at those who grow rich in this age, for they too will leave it all behind, and go out naked. *“Be not thou afraid,”* says David, *“when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him”* [Psalm 48:17–18].

Riches in themselves are a good thing, and do no harm to a man, but bring profit; whether harm or profit comes of riches depends on the man himself: such as the man who has them is, such will his riches be to him, either harmful or profitable. So wine is medicine to the wise, but poison to the fool; a sword is a defence to the good man, but ruin to the wicked, both to himself and to others; fire, too, brings both profit and harm: profit to him who uses it with care, and harm to him who handles it carelessly, or uses it to his neighbour's hurt. Reason itself is both profitable and harmful: profitable to him who uses it for his own good and his neighbour's, and harmful to him who uses it to his neighbour's hurt, and so, consequently, to his own, for a man cannot harm his neighbour without greater harm to himself. So it is, too, with riches: they become such as the heart of the man who has them. But since man has a corrupted heart, and cannot bear prosperity with moderation, for the most part riches do him harm — not from their own side, but from the man's, who cannot use a good thing rightly.

Therefore the apostle says: *“They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare,”* and the rest. Therefore the Lord teaches that *“it is hard for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven,”* and says further: *“It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God”* [Matthew 19:23–24]. Therefore the Wise Man prays: *“Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: lest I be full, and deny Thee, and say, Who is the Lord? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain”* [Proverbs 30:8–9]. And David, though rich and glorious, prays to God: *“Incline my heart unto Thy testimonies, and not to covetousness”* [Psalm 118:36]. And he exhorted others too: *“If riches increase, set not your heart”* upon them [Psalm 61:11]. And the apostle exhorts: *“The time is short... and they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away”* [1 Corinthians 7:29, 31].

Consider, beloved, and reflect upon the apostle's words: *“They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition”* — and upon Christ's words: “It is hard for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven” — and take care not to grow rich, lest riches drown you in the deep.

7) And if you have riches, spend them as the Word of God teaches. Be exactly assured that the Christian inheritance is hidden in the heavens, and is incomparably better than the earthly and the temporal — and then you will count all that is earthly and temporal as nothing, and will strain with constant longing toward the eternal. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also [Matthew 6:21]. As the sons of this age choose gold and silver above copper, so the sons of the kingdom, true Christians, having despised all the treasures of this world, strain with all their desire toward the things above. There is their fatherland, and their inheritance, and their riches, and their glory, and their honour, and their home, and all their treasure is there. There is the supper prepared, and the marriage, and the comfort, and the gladness, and the joy. There the festal and bridal garment awaits them. There the Heavenly Father awaits them, and the choirs of the saints: *“Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God”* [Luke 14:15]. Yet *“many are called, but few are chosen”* [Luke 14:24].

Let us strive, beloved, to be not only among the called, but among the chosen, that we too may be found worthy to eat and drink at Christ's table in His kingdom [Luke 22:30]. O Lord, grant it! O Lord, bring us there! O Merciful One, have mercy, and hear us!

But we must first taste bitterness, and suffer with Christ, as the apostle says [2 Timothy 2:12]. *“Ye have continued with Me in My temptations.* *And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as My Father hath appointed unto Me, that ye may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom”* [Luke 22:28–30]. How sweet it will be to eat and drink at that table! But the enchantment of riches, of vain glory, of luxury and of pleasures, draws the poor man away from it.

*“Open thou mine eyes”* [Psalm 108:18], O man, and know the enchantment. Turn away your eyes, your mind and your heart from the earth, and turn them toward the heavens. Be exactly assured that you are a stranger and a sojourner here, and then you will know the enchantment, and will be content with what you have, though it be little, and will use everything in the world with fear, as a stranger and a sojourner. For who burdens himself on a journey? Does he not rather cast off every burden, that he may travel the lighter? Who hides up a treasure for himself in a foreign land? Does he not rather send it on ahead to his own fatherland? You are on a journey, and in a foreign land, O Christian! You are called to the heavenly Jerusalem, and there God has shown you your fatherland. Why, then, on the road, and in a foreign land, would you wish to grow rich? For you will not take this riches with you there, but will leave it all here, in the foreign land. There an incorruptible and inalienable riches is prepared, not for the lovers of silver and gold, but for *“them that love God”* [1 Corinthians 2:9].

9) If anyone has riches justly gained — though this is a rare thing — and spends it not on luxury, on excessive buildings and other vanity, but is himself content with it in moderation, and provides for the churches of God, for almshouses and for the poor, and *“is not highminded, nor trusteth in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that he do good, that he be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate,”* and the rest [1 Timothy 6:17–18] — to such a man riches not only does no harm, but brings profit as well.
10) If anyone has gathered riches unjustly, he must justly disperse what he has gathered to his neighbour's wrong, following the example of Zacchaeus the publican [Luke 19:8].
Be saved.
